readings.c1s1:
¶
'''beguile''' (bē-gīl′), ''v. t.'' [‹ ME. ''begilen'', ''begylen'' (= MD. ''beghijlen''), < ''be-'' + ''gilen'', ''gylen'', guile, deceive: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''guile''.] '''1.''' To delude with guile; deceive; impose on by artifice or craft.
{{smaller block|The serpent ''beguiled'' me, and I did eat. {{right|Gen. iii. 13.}}
<poem>By expectation every day ''beguil’d'',
Dupe of to-morrow even from a child.</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', My Mother’s Picture.}}}}
'''2.''' To elude or check by artifice or craft; foil.
{{smaller block|<poem>’Twas yet some comfort,
When misery could ''beguile'' the tyrant’s rage,
And frustrate his proud will.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, iv. 6.}}}}
'''3.''' To deprive of irksomeness or unpleasantness by diverting the mind; render unfelt; cause to pass insensibly and pleasantly; while away.
{{smaller block|<poem>I would ''beguile''
The tedious day with sleep.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iii. 2.}}
<poem>Chiefs of elder Art!
Teachers of wisdom! who could once ''beguile''
My tedious hours.</poem>
{{right|''Roscoe'', To my Books.}}}}
'''4.''' To transform as if by charm or guile; charm.
{{smaller block|<poem>Till to a smile
The goodwife’s tearful face he did ''beguile''.</poem>
{{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, II. 225.}}}}
'''5.''' To entertain as with pastimes; amuse.
{{smaller block|<poem>The tales
With which this day the children she ''beguiled''
She glean’d from Breton grandames when a child.</poem>
{{right|''M. Arnold'', Tristram and Iseult, iii.}}}}
'''To beguile of''', to deprive of by guile or pleasing artifice.
{{smaller block|The writer who ''beguiles of'' their tediousness the dull hours of life. {{right|''Everett'', Orations, I. 302.}}}}
='''Syn. 1.''' Cheat, mislead, inveigle.—'''3-5.''' ''Amuse'', ''Divert'', etc. (see ''amuse''); cheer, solace.

¶
'''beguinage''' (beg′in-ạ̄j, or, as mod. F., bā-gē-näzh′), ''n.'' [F. ''béguinage'', OF. ''beguinage'' (> ML. ''beghinagium''), < ''beguine'', a Beguine. See ''Beguin'' and ''-age''.] A community of Beguines. {{smaller|A beguinage usually consists of a large walled inclosure, containing a number of small detached houses, each inhabited by one or two Beguines; there are also some common houses, especially for the novices and younger members of the community. In the center is the church, where certain religious offices are performed in common. Each Beguine keeps possession of her own property, and may support herself from it, or from the work of her hands, or by serving others in their houses. They are free to leave at any time, and take only simple vows of chastity and obedience during residence. Pious women may also, under certain restrictions, rent houses and live inside the inclosure without formally joining the community. Such establishments are now chiefly met with in Belgium; the immense one near Ghent, built by the Duke of Aremberg in 1874, is the finest example, and one of the most recent.}}

'''Beguine''', ''n.'' See ''Beguin''.

'''begum'''<sup>1</sup> (bē-gum′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''begummed'', ppr. ''begumming''. [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''gum''<sup>2</sup>.] To daub or cover with gum. ''Swift.''

'''begum'''<sup>2</sup> (bē′gum), ''n.'' [Anglo-Ind., also ''beegum'', ''begaum'', < Hind. ''begam'' (cf. Pers. ''baigīm'', a lady), < Turki ''bigīm'', a princess, fem. of ''big'', ''bik'' = Turk. ''beg'', ''bey'', a prince: see ''bey''<sup>1</sup>.] The title of a Hindu princess or lady of high rank.

'''begun''' (bẹ̄-gun′). Past participle and sometimes preterit of ''begin''.

'''begunk''' (bẹ̄-gungk′), ''v. t.'' [Also spelled ''begink'', perhaps a nasalized variation of equiv. Sc. ''begeck'', q. v. See also remark under ''beflum''.] To befool; deceive; balk; jilt. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|Whose sweetheart has ''begunked'' him.
{{right|''Blackwood’s Mag.'', VIII. 426.}}}}

'''Beguin, Beguine''' (beg′in; sometimes, as mod. F., bā-gaṅ′, m., -gēn′, f.), ''n.''   [(1) ''Beguin, Beguine'', fem.: early mod. E. also ''begin, begine, beghine, beggin, bigin, biggayne'', < ME. ''begyne, bygynne'', < OF. ''beguine'', mod. F. ''béguine'' = Sp. Pg. ''beguina'' = It. ''beghina, bighina'' (MD. ''beghijne'', D. ''begijn'', LG. and G. ''begine''), < ML. ''beghina, begina, beggina, beguina, bigina'', etc. (cf. E. ''biggin''<sup>1</sup>, from the same source). (2) ''Beguin'', masc., < OF. ''beguin'', mod. F. ''béguin'' = Sp. Pg. ''beguino'' = It. ''beghino, bighino'', < ML. ''beghinus, beginus, begginus, beguinus, biginus'', etc.: formed, first as fem., with suffix ''-in'', ML. ''-ina, -inus'', from the name of Lambert ''Begue'' or ''le Begue'' (i. e., the stammerer: OF. ''begue'', mod. F. ''bègue'', dial. ''beique, bieque'', stammering; of unknown origin), a priest of Liège, who founded the sisterhood. See also ''Beghard''. The origin of the name was not generally known, and the forms varied, leading to many etymological conjectures. The connection with E. ''beggar'' and ''beg''<sup>1</sup> is perhaps real; in the sense of ‘hypocrite’ and ‘bigot’ (as in It. ''beghino''), the word was later confused with ''bigot'', q. v.]   '''1.''' A name given to the members of various religious communities of women who, professing a life of poverty and self-denial, went about in coarse gray clothing (of undyed wool), reading the Scriptures and exhorting the people. {{smaller|They originated in the twelfth or thirteenth century, and formerly flourished in Germany, the Netherlands, France, and Italy; and communities of the name still exist in Belgium. See ''beguinage''. [Now generally written ''Beguine''.]}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And Dame Abstinence streyned,
Toke on a robe of kamelyne,
And gan her graithe [dress] as a ''bygynne''.</poem>
{{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 7366.}}}}
{{smaller block|Wanton wenches and ''beguins''.
{{right|''World of Wonders'', 1608.}}}}
{{smaller block|The wife of one of the ex-burgomasters and his daughter, who was a ''beguin'', went by his side as he was led to execution. {{right|''Motley'', Dutch Republic, II. 442.}}}}
'''2.''' [Only ''Beguin''.] A member of a community of men founded on the same general principle of life as that of the Beguines (see 1). {{smaller|They became infected with various heresies, especially with systems of illuminism, which were afterward propagated among the communities of women. They were condemned by Pope John XXII. in the early part of the fourteenth century. The faithful Beguins joined themselves in numbers with the different orders of friars. The sect, generally obnoxious and the object of severe measures, had greatly diminished by the following century, but continued to exist till about the middle of the sixteenth. Also called ''Beghard''. [These names have been frequently used as common nouns, without capitals.]}}

See ''Beguin'' and ''-age''.]   A community of Beguines. {{smaller|A beguinage usually consists of a large walled inclosure, containing a number of small detached houses, each inhabited by one or two Beguines; there are also some common houses, especially for the novices and younger members of the community. In the center is the church, where certain religious offices are performed in common. They are free to leave at any time, and take only simple vows of chastity and obedience during residence. Pious women may also, under certain restrictions, rent houses and live inside the inclosure without formally joining the community. Such establishments are now chiefly met with in Belgium; the immense one near Ghent, built by the Duke of Aremberg in 1874, is the finest example, and one of the most recent.}}

'''Beguine''', ''n.'' See ''Beguin''.

'''begum'''<sup>1</sup> (bē-gum′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''begummed'', ppr. ''begumming''.   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''gum''<sup>2</sup>.]   To daub or cover with gum.   ''Swift.''

'''begum'''<sup>2</sup> (bē′gum), ''n.''   [Anglo-Ind., also ''beegum'', ''begaum'', < Hind. ''begam'' (cf. Pers. ''baigīm'', a lady), < Turki ''bigīm'', a princess, fem. of ''big'', ''bik'' = Turk. ''beg'', ''bey'', a prince: see ''bey''<sup>1</sup>.]   The title of a Hindu princess or lady of high rank.

'''begun''' (bẹ̄-gun′). Past participle and sometimes preterit of ''begin''.

'''begunk''' (bẹ̄-gungk′), ''v. t.''   [Also spelled ''begink'', perhaps a nasalized variation of equiv. Sc. ''begeck'', q. v. See also remark under ''beflum''.]   To befool; deceive; balk; jilt. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|Whose sweetheart has ''begunked'' him.

'''begunk''' (bē-gungk′), ''n.''   [< ''begunk'', ''v.'']   An illusion; a trick; a cheat. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|If I havena’ gien Inchgrabbit and Jamie Howie a bonnie ''begunk'', they ken themsel’s. {{right|''Scott'', Waverley, II. xxxv.}}}}

'''behad''' (bē-häd′), ''a.''   [Contr. of Sc. *''behald'' = E. ''beholden''.]   Beholden; indebted. [Scotch.]

'''behalf''' (bē-häf′), ''n.''   [< ME. ''behalve'', ''bihalve'', in the phrase ''on'' (or ''upon'', or ''in'') ''behalve'', in behalf, incorrectly used for ''on halve'' (< AS. ''on healfe'', on the side or part of), owing to confusion with ME. ''behalve'', ''behalven'', ''behalves'', adv. and prep., by the side of, near, < AS. ''be healfe'', by the side: see ''be-''<sup>2</sup>, ''by''<sup>1</sup>, and ''half'', ''n.'' Cf. ''behoof''.]   '''1.''' Advantage, benefit, interest, or defense (of somebody or something).
{{smaller block|In the ''behalf'' of his mistress’s beauty. {{right|''Sir P. Sidney.''}}}}
{{smaller block|I was moved to speak in ''behalf'' of the absent. {{right|''Sumner'', Prison Discipline.}}}}
'''2†.''' Affair; cause; matter.
{{smaller block|In an unjust ''behalf.'' {{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., i. 3.}}}}
[Always governed by the preposition ''in'', ''on'', or ''upon''. See note under ''behoof''.]—'''In this''' or '''that behalf''', {{smaller|in respect of, or with regard to, this or that matter.}}

'''behap†''' (bē-hap′), ''v. i.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''hap''<sup>1</sup>.]   To happen.

'''behappen†''' (bē-hap′n), ''v. i.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''happen'', appar. suggested by ''befall''.]   To happen.
{{smaller block|<poem>That is the greatest shame, and foulest scorne,
Which unto any knight ''behappen'' may.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., V. xi. 52.}}}}

'''behate†''', ''v. t.''   [ME.; < ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''hate''.]   To hate; detest.   ''Chaucer.''

'''behave''' (bē-hāv′), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''behaved'', ppr. ''behaving''.   [< late ME. ''behaven'', restrain, refl. behave (see first quot.), < ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''have'' (which thus compounded took the full inflections (pret. rarely ''behad'' and irreg. ''beheft'') and developed reg. into the mod. pron. hāv). The word is formally identical with AS. ''behabban'', hold, surround, restrain (= OS. ''bihebbian'', hold, surround, = OHG. ''bihabēn'', MHG. ''behaben'', hold, take possession of), < ''be'', about, + ''habban'', have, hold: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''have''.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1†.''' To govern; manage; conduct; regulate.
{{smaller block|<poem>To Florence they can hur kenne,
To lerne hur to ''behave'' hur among men.</poem>
{{right|''Le Bone Florence'', l. 1567.}}}}
{{smaller block|He did ''behave'' his anger ere ’twas spent.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. of A., iii. 5.}}}}
[The old editions read ''behoove'' in this passage.] —'''2.''' With a reflexive pronoun, to conduct, comport, acquit, or demean. (''a'') In some specified way.
{{smaller block|Those that ''behaved themselves'' manfully. {{right|2 Mac. ii. 21.}}}}
{{smaller block|We ''behaved'' not ''ourselves'' disorderly among you.
{{right|2 Thes. iii. 7.}}}}
(''b'') Absolutely, in a commendable or proper way; well or properly: as, ''behave yourself; they'' will not ''behave themselves''.—'''3†.''' To employ or occupy.
{{smaller block|<poem>Where ease abownds yt’s eath to doe amis:
But who his limbs with labours, and his mynd
''Behaves'' with cares, cannot so easy mis.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. iii. 40.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' [The reflexive pronoun omitted.] To act in any relation; have or exhibit a mode of action or conduct: used of persons, and also of things having motion or operation. (''a'') In a particular manner, as specified: as, to ''behave'' well or ill; the ship ''behaves'' well.
{{smaller block|But he was wiser and well ''beheft''.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Love’s Welcome at Welbeck.}}}}
{{smaller block|Electricity ''behaves'' like an incompressible fluid.
{{right|''Atkinson'', tr. of Mascart and Joubert, I. 110.}}}}
(''b'') Absolutely, in a proper manner: as, why do you not ''behave?''

'''behaved''' (bē-hāvd′), ''p. a.'' Mannered; conducted: usually with some qualifying adverb: as, a well-''behaved'' person.
{{smaller block|<poem>Gather by him, as he is ''behav’d'',
If ’t be the affliction of his love, or no,
That thus he suffers for. {{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iii. 1.}}</poem>
Why, I take the French-''behaved'' gentleman.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Cynthia’s Revels, v. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|A very pretty ''behaved'' gentleman.
{{right|''Sheridan'', The Rivals, v. 1.}}}}

'''behavior, behaviour''' (bē-hāv′yor), ''n.''   [The latter spelling is usual in England; early mod. E. ''behavoure'', ''behavior'', ''behavier'', ''behaviour'', ''behaver, behavor, behavour'', < ''behave'' + ''-oure, -iour, -ior'', appar. in simulation of ''havior, haviour, havour'', var. of ''haver'' for ''aver'', possession, having (see ''aver''<sup>2</sup>), of F. origin. In poetry sometimes ''havior'', which may be taken as formed directly from ''have;'' cf. Sc. ''have'', behave, ''havings'', behavior.]   '''1.''' Manner of behaving, whether good or bad; conduct; mode of acting; manners; deportment: sometimes, when used absolutely, implying good breeding or proper deportment.
{{smaller block|Some men’s ''behaviour'' is like a verse wherein every syllable is measured.
{{right|''Bacon'', Essays, Of Ceremonies and Respects.}}}}
{{smaller block|A gentleman that is very singular in his ''behaviour.''
{{right|''Steele.''}}}}
'''2.''' Figuratively, the manner in which anything acts or operates.
{{smaller block|The ''behaviour'' of the nitrous salts of the amines is worthy of attention. ''Austen-Pinner'', Org. Chem., p. 46.

The phenomena of electricity and magnetism were reduced to the same category; and the ''behaviour'' of the magnetic needle was assimilated to that of a needle subjected to the influence of artificial electric currents.
{{right|''H. Spencer'', Prin. of Psychol.}}}}
'''3†.''' The act of representing another person; the manner in which one personates the character of another; representative character. {{smaller|[Very rare, possibly unique. Knight, however, believes that the word is used here in its natural sense, that is, the manner of ''having'' or conducting one’s self.]}}
{{smaller block|''King John.'' Now, say, Chatillon, what would France with us?}}

<poem>''Chat.'' Thus, after greeting, speaks the king of France,
In my ''behaviour'', to the majesty,
The borrow’d majesty, of England here.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, i. 1.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Behavior as heir''' (law Latin, ''gestio pro hærede''), in ''Scots law'', a passive title, by which an heir, by intromission with his ancestor’s heritage, incurs a universal liability for his debts and obligations.—'''During good behavior,''' as long as one remains blameless in the discharge of one’s duties or the conduct of one’s life: as, an office held ''during good behavior''; a convict is given certain privileges ''during good behavior''.—'''On one’s behavior''' or '''good behavior.''' (''a'') Behaving or bound to behave with a regard to conventional decorum and propriety. [Colloq.] (''b'') In a state of probation; liable to be called to account in case of misconduct.}}

{{smaller block|Tyrants themselves are ''upon their behaviour'' to a superior power. {{right|''Sir R. L’Estrange'', Fables.}}}}

{{smaller|='''Syn. 1.''' ''Carriage, Behavior, Conduct, Deportment, Demeanor'', bearing, manner, manners, all denote primarily outward manner or conduct, but naturally are freely extended to internal states or activities. ''Carriage'', the way of carrying one’s self, may be mere physical attitude, or it may be personal manners, as expressing states of mind: we speak of a haughty or noble ''carriage'', but not ordinarily of an ignoble, cringing, or base ''carriage''. ''Behavior'' is the most general expression of one’s mode of acting; it also refers particularly to comparatively conspicuous actions and conduct. ''Conduct'' is more applicable to actions viewed as connected into a course of life, especially to actions considered with reference to morality. ''Deportment'' is especially behavior in the line of the proprieties or duties of life: as, Mr. Turveydrop was a model of ''deportment''; the scholars’ rank depends partly upon their ''deportment''. ''Demeanor'' is most used for manners as expressing character; it is a more delicate word than the others, and is generally used in a good sense. We may speak of lofty or gracious ''carriage''; good, bad, wise, foolish, modest, conceited ''behavior''; exemplary ''conduct''; grand, modest, correct ''deportment''; quiet, refined ''demeanor''.}}

{{smaller block|Nothing can be more delicate without being fantastical, nothing more firm and based in nature and sentiment, than the courtship and mutual ''carriage'' of the sexes [in England].
{{right|''Emerson'', Eng. Traits, p. 112.}}}}

{{smaller block|Men’s ''behaviour'' should be like their apparel, not too strait or point-device, but free for exercise or motion.
{{right|''Bacon'', Essays, liii.}}}}

{{smaller block|It is both more satisfactory and more safe to trust to the ''conduct'' of a party than their professions.
{{right|''Ames'', Works, II. 214.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
